source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 244: definition of uniform integrability for 'a collection of random variables X_i, i in I'; remark that choosing M with sup < 1 gives sup_i E|X_i| <= M+1 < infinity.
source_check.comparison: Tail formula, uniform small-event control, E(Z;A) notation, empty-family convention and version convention are supplied (body 15-35); the M+1 bound is proved (annex 5-7). Narrowed variant: the handbook defines the property only for 'real integrable random variables' (body 17-18), whereas Durrett's definition applies to any collection and his remark makes integrability a consequence of uniform integrability. No on-route text states or proves that consequence for an arbitrary family.

components.gap: C001 (def:p15-uniform-integrability, body 15-35): the definition presupposes integrable variables. Supply Durrett's variant (p. 244): uniform integrability for an arbitrary family of real random variables (tail expectations in [0,infinity]), with the written step that it forces integrability and sup_i E|X_i| <= M+1.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 244: M+1 remark; 'trivial example' of a family dominated by an integrable Y; small-event property inside the proof of Thm 4.6.1.
source_check.comparison: Both directions of the equivalence proved (annex 6-20), with the C=0 boundary (16-17) and the empty family (5); domination (22-26), finite families (26-27) and the first-moment counterexample (27-30) proved.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 245, Thm 4.6.2: phi >= 0 any function with phi(x)/x -> infinity (e.g. x^p, p > 1, or x log+ x); if E phi(|X_i|) <= C for all i then {X_i} is uniformly integrable; proof via eps_M = sup{x/phi(x): x >= M}.
source_check.comparison: The forward bound (annex 36-44), both examples (body 52-54, annex 45-46), the C=0 and empty-family boundaries (44, 72) and the de la Vallee Poussin converse (48-72) are written. Narrowed variant: through the definition (body 17-18) the criterion applies only to a family already known to be integrable. Durrett's theorem has no integrability hypothesis and concludes uniform integrability, hence integrability. The handbook never writes the step from the moment bound to integrability.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 244, Thm 4.6.1 (X in L1; all sigma-fields F contained in F_o) and proof; remark that uniformly integrable families 'can be very large'.
source_check.comparison: Same statement over all sub-sigma-algebras; 'no nesting or countability assumption' carries the 'very large' remark. Proof steps written: small-event delta, Markov bound on V_G, conditional Jensen, defining identity, and the E|X|=0 boundary (annex 78-94).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 246, Lemma 4.6.5. Also the Chapter 2 facts his Section 4.6 proofs invoke (Lemma 2.2.2, Thm 2.3.2, Exercises 2.3.4-2.3.5); these are outside the required pages and are proved here.
source_check.comparison: All five assertions proved. The event-integral item gives Lemma 4.6.5 uniformly in A. The K=0, infinite and zero lower-limit boundaries are handled.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett pp. 245-246, Thm 4.6.3 (E|X_n| < infinity, X_n -> X in probability; (i) {X_n: n >= 0} UI, (ii) X_n -> X in L1, (iii) E|X_n| -> E|X| < infinity) and proof with the clipping phi_M and the cutoff psi_M.
source_check.comparison: Same hypotheses and the same three conditions; (ii) makes X in L1 explicit, which is implied. Both source truncations are retained, with psi_M written out (annex 167-176). Every implication is proved, including the step for finitely many early terms (191-195).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 246, Thm 4.6.4 (submartingale: UI, a.s. and L1, L1 equivalent) and proof.
source_check.comparison: All three equivalences proved by the source route (martingale convergence, then Vitali). Additions are proved: the supermartingale sign change, an F_infinity-measurable limit version and the terminal inequality X_n <= E(X_infinity|F_n) (annex 212-222).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 247, Thm 4.6.7(iv): an integrable X with X_n = E(X|F_n).
source_check.comparison: The definition matches condition (iv). Boundary: Z need not be F_infinity-measurable, and its observable part E(Z|F_infinity) is identified in the annex (239-256).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett pp. 246-247: Lemmas 4.6.5-4.6.6 and Thm 4.6.7 with proofs.
source_check.comparison: The four equivalences are proved. Lemma 4.6.6 (an L1 limit closes the martingale) is proved at annex 229-235, and (iv)=>(i) by the conditional-family theorem at 236-237. The extra identification X_infinity = E(Z|F_infinity) is proved by pi-lambda (239-256).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 247, Thm 4.6.8 and proof.
source_check.comparison: Same hypotheses and conclusion. Each step of the source route is written: tower martingale, UI, closed-martingale convergence, pi-lambda identification. The limit is defined on the exceptional set (273-274).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett pp. 247-248, Thm 4.6.9 (Levy's 0-1 law) and its continuation: the line borrowed from Chung (judge whether the result is obvious or incredible); the 'obvious' reading (1_A in F_infinity and F_n increase to F_infinity, so the best guess of 1_A given F_n should approach 1_A, the best guess given F_infinity); the 'incredible' reading (Kolmogorov's 0-1 law); the closing judgement that the argument may not show the result is 'too unusual or improbable to be possible', but this and later applications show it is very useful.
source_check.comparison: Supplied: the statement (the handbook adds L1 convergence), the name through \index (body 175), and the complete Kolmogorov/'incredible' argument (annex 293-303). Absent from the route: the Chung attribution, the 'obvious' justificatory reading and the closing evaluative judgement.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 248, Thm 4.6.10 'Dominated convergence theorem for conditional expectations' (Y_n -> Y a.s., |Y_n| <= Z, EZ < infinity, F_n increase to F_infinity => E(Y_n|F_n) -> E(Y|F_infinity) a.s.) with the W_N proof; p. 249, Exercise 4.6.7.
source_check.comparison: Hypotheses, the a.s. conclusion and the W_N proof are written (annex 321-347). Exercise 4.6.7 (309-317) and L1 convergence under domination (318-319) are proved. Absent: the source's name for the theorem. The entry title, its index and the generated named-theorem index never call it the dominated convergence theorem for conditional expectations. On the route, 'conditional dominated convergence' names the fixed-sigma-field result thm:p15-conditional-limits(3) (annex 339; conditional-expectation.tex 101-104).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 248, Example 4.6.11 (Y_n, Z_n independent; P(Y_n=1)=1/n, P(Z_n=n)=1/n; X_n = Y_n Z_n; F = sigma(Y_1, Y_2, ...)). Its preamble: UI and a.s. convergence give E(X_n|F) -> E(X|F) in L1 via Thm 4.6.3 and Exercise 4.6.7.
source_check.comparison: The construction is equivalent (B_n = Y_n, nC_n = Z_n). Written in full: P(X_n>0) = 1/n^2 with Borel-Cantelli, a complete tail computation for UI (annex 373-377), E(X_n|G) = B_n, and L1 but not a.s. convergence by both Borel-Cantelli lemmas (383-388). The preamble's general claim combines thm:p15-vitali-convergence and thm:p15-changing-conditional-limits(1), both on the route. The extra examples (1) and (2) are proved.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 249: Omega = [0,1), I_{k,n} = [k2^-n, (k+1)2^-n), F_n = sigma(I_{k,n}: 0 <= k < 2^n).
source_check.comparison: Same objects, with Borel sets and uniform probability explicit. Boundaries: atom mass and the right endpoint 1. Nesting and generation of the Borel sets are proved at annex 394-402.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 249, Exercise 4.6.2 (Lipschitz f, dyadic slopes a martingale, X_n -> X_infinity a.s. and in L1, f(b)-f(a) = int_a^b X_infinity) and Exercise 4.6.3 (E(f|F_n) a step function converging to f in L1, hence step approximation). Exercise 4.6.3 adds: 'This approximation is much simpler than the bare-hands approach we used in Exercise 1.4.3, but of course we are using a lot of machinery.'
source_check.comparison: All mathematics is written, including the extension to the endpoint 1, the completed-Lebesgue extension and general endpoints (annex 404-454). Absent from the route: Exercise 4.6.3's comparative claim. Exercise 1.4.3 itself is proved elsewhere on the route (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02b-p15-001.tex 473-476), but no on-route text compares the two routes. The body's claim 'These are the complete source Exercises 4.6.2--3' (line 253) is therefore not yet met.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 248, Exercise 4.6.1: Z_i i.i.d. with E|Z_i| < infinity; theta an independent r.v. with finite mean; Y_i = Z_i + theta. 'If Z_i is normal(0,1) then in statistical terms we have a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean.' The distribution of theta is called the prior distribution, and P(theta in . | Y_1,...,Y_n) the posterior distribution after n observations. Show E(theta|Y_1,...,Y_n) -> theta a.s.
source_check.comparison: Hypotheses and conclusion supplied and proved (the handbook adds L1 convergence), and the normal case is asserted (body 266; annex 476-477). Absent from the entry: the statistical reading of the normal case (a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean theta) and the source's definitions of the prior distribution (law of theta) and the posterior distribution P(theta in . | Y_1,...,Y_n), which make E(theta|F_n) the posterior mean. The entry uses 'prior variable' and 'posterior consistency' without defining them.

components.gap: C016 (thm:p15-posterior-mean-consistency, body 256-270; annex 458-479): Exercise 4.6.1's (p. 248) statistical reading and terminology are absent. Supply: with normal(0,1) noise the Y_i are a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean theta; the law of theta is the prior distribution; P(theta in . | Y_1,...,Y_n) is the posterior distribution after n observations, so E(theta|Y_1,...,Y_n) is the posterior mean.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 249, Exercises 4.6.4 (X_n in [0,infinity), D = {X_n = 0 for some n >= 1}, P(D|X_1..X_n) >= delta(x) > 0 a.s. on {X_n <= x} => P(D or lim X_n = infinity) = 1) and 4.6.5 (branching process, p_0 > 0 => P(lim Z_n = 0 or infinity) = 1).
source_check.comparison: The hypothesis is equivalent: integer thresholds K versus Durrett's real x (specialise x = K; conversely use K = ceil(x)). The conclusion is proved via Levy's event theorem. The branching case generalises Z_0, with the m = 0 case, initial extinction and no mean assumption handled (annex 493-513).

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 249, Exercise 4.6.6 (X_n in [0,1] adapted; alpha, beta > 0, alpha+beta = 1; the two conditional probabilities; P(lim X_n = 0 or 1) = 1, and X_0 = theta gives P(lim X_n = 1) = theta).
source_check.comparison: Equivalent parameter range (0 < alpha, beta < 1). Both conclusions are proved, the second in the stronger form EX_0, with the deterministic case stated. The hypotheses are shown realisable.

source_check.required_extent_compared: Durrett p. 249, opening of Section 4.7: 'A backwards martingale (some authors call them reversed) is a martingale indexed by the negative integers ... E(X_{n+1}|F_n) = X_n for n <= -1. Because the sigma-fields decrease as n decreases to -infinity, the convergence theory for backwards martingales is particularly simple.'
source_check.comparison: Supplied: the definition in nonnegative reverse-time indices and its exact translation to the source's negative indices (body 326-328). Absent from the text: the alternative name 'reversed', present only as \index{martingale!reverse} (line 329); and the justificatory claim that decreasing sigma-fields make the convergence theory particularly simple.
